tip: 'Acabar' = to finish, so 'acabamos de mudarnos' is literally 'we finish from moving' – Spanish's way of saying 'just did'. Present tense, past meaning.
Your body isn't 'yours' in Spanish: 'la oreja', not 'mi oreja'. 'Me duele' already says whose ear hurts – adding 'mi' would sound oddly possessive.
Subjunctive after 'quiero que': 'coman' (not 'comen').
'Quieres' and 'lleve' have different subjects – that switch forces 'que' + subjunctive. If YOU wanted to bring it, it'd be plain '¿quieres llevarlo?', no 'que' at all.
'Antes de que' (before) always takes subjunctive – the event hasn't happened yet.
'¿Podría...?' is the workplace-safe ask: conditional 'could you' softens the request. 'Podría enviarme' + 'por favor' = polished formal; 'puedes' would sound chummy.
'Para' + 'ser' + profession = purpose/goal.
'Por una semana' – 'por' for duration of time. How long the rental lasted.
Spanish doubles up on purpose: 'le' already means 'to her', yet 'a mi madre' still appears. Not redundant – 'le' is grammar glue, 'a mi madre' the clarifier.
'Por' = in exchange for: 'Cambié mi coche por uno nuevo.' 'Por' for swapping one thing for another.
'Quedar' normally means 'to remain' – but between friends, 'quedamos' = we meet up. 'Quedamos los viernes' is making Friday plans, not staying home.
'Por' + person = on behalf of, for the sake of.
'Recuerdos' means memories AND greetings: 'dale recuerdos' = 'give her my regards', the standard warm sign-off. 'De mi parte' ('from my side') makes it personal.
Preterite flips 'conocer' from 'know' to 'meet': 'conocí a mi mejor amigo' = I MET him. Knowing is ongoing; the preterite pinpoints the moment it began.
'Ni que' + past subjunctive = sarcastic 'as if!': 'ni que fueras el único' = 'it's not like you're the only one'. Literally 'not even if you were'.
'Por más que' + subjunctive = no matter how much.
Double subjunctive: 'estudien' (after 'quiero que') and 'guste' (after 'lo que' – 'whatever they like' isn't a known thing yet, so it goes subjunctive too).
'Me' is indirect object – music pleases me.
'Por ti' = for your sake, because of you. 'Para ti' would mean it's destined to be handed to you. Both translate 'for you' – Spanish makes you pick the why or the where-to.
Why not 'llegas'? Future-time 'cuando' takes subjunctive – getting home hasn't happened yet. 'Cuando llegues' = whenever that turns out to be.
'Habrá' is the future of 'haber' – used here for speculation.
Affirmative was 'olvídate'; add 'no' and the command flips: the pronoun jumps in front and the verb turns subjunctive – 'no te olvides'.
Reflexive 'tú' command: 'ponte' = Put on (yourself). Irregular command 'pon' + reflexive 'te' attached.
'Para' + infinitive for purpose / goal.
Who must get up? Nobody named: 'hay que' states duty with no subject at all. 'Hay que madrugar' = early rising is required, for whoever's listening.
No 'for' needed: 'pedir' already means 'ask for'. You request the thing directly – 'pedí un aumento' – and the person just takes 'le'/'a'. 'Pedir por' is a different beast.
Surprise: 'si' resists the subjunctive. Real, open conditions take plain present – 'si no trabajas' – never 'si trabajes'. Save subjunctive for unreal ifs.
'¿Puedo llamarte?' isn't really about ability – it's asking permission, just like English 'can I'. 'Poder' does both jobs: capability and polite requests.
Spanish has no everyday verb for 'lock'. You close 'con llave' – with a key. Drop 'con llave' and 'cierro la puerta' is just shutting the door, not locking it.
'Que tenga' – subjunctive after 'decir que' (telling someone to do something).
